article.overview: A far-side radio observatory is a radio telescope placed on the lunar farside, the hemisphere that always faces away from Earth. Its purpose is to detect radio waves at frequencies that are hard or impossible to study from Earth. Those low frequencies, roughly below 50 MHz in the sources reviewed, are blocked or distorted by Earth's ionosphere. Earth's own radio transmissions also make the sky noisy. The farside is shielded from both, which makes it an attractive place for very faint, early-universe signals. The concept is currently represented by one planned flight instrument, LuSEE-Night, and by a proposed large array, FARSIDE. Earlier radio instruments with far-side or lunar-orbit placements provide partial precedents.
article.description: A far-side radio observatory consists of radio antennas, a receiver or spectrometer, a digitiser and a timing and data system. Some concepts also include a base station, a rover or deployment mechanism, and a relay link to Earth. The antennas are usually long, thin elements (dipoles) or small arrays of them, and their length is matched to the wavelengths of interest. At 10 MHz the free-space wavelength is about 30 m, so the antennas must be large in wavelength terms even when they are only metres long physically. Two broad architectures appear in the sources. The first is a single-site pathfinder: a small set of antennas and a receiver on one lander, of which LuSEE-Night is the planned example, designed to test the lunar environment and the measurement technique. The second is an interferometric array: many antennas spread over kilometres, combined electronically to make images of the radio sky, of which FARSIDE is the proposed example, deployed by a rover and supported by a base station.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main science goals in the reviewed sources are the following. Cosmic Dark Ages: the period before the first stars, which the Berkeley Lab article describes as roughly 400 million years long; a faint, redshifted 21 cm hydrogen signal from that era is the main target of LuSEE-Night, and its detection would require careful calibration because foreground emission from the Galaxy is much brighter. Solar and heliospheric radio bursts: low-frequency bursts from the Sun and from coronal mass ejections can be monitored, and the FARSIDE concept lists near-continuous monitoring of stellar systems and solar-system radio activity among its goals (Burns et al., 2019). Planetary radio emission: emission from Jupiter and the outer planets is a stated target for NCLE and the LuSEE programme (Burns et al., 2021; IEEE Spectrum, 2019). Lunar subsurface and plasma environment: the FARSIDE concept lists sounding of the lunar subsurface, and the LuSEE programme includes measurement of local plasma and exo-ionospheric density (Burns et al., 2021). These are scientific aims. None of them has been shown by a published measurement in the sources reviewed.
article.operating_principle: A radio telescope on the Moon detects electric fields with antennas. An incoming wave induces a small voltage across the antenna. The receiver amplifies this voltage, filters it to a chosen band, and digitises it. A spectrometer computes the power in many frequency channels over time. Because the signal is so faint, calibration matters as much as antenna design: the instrument must separate the sky signal from its own electronics, from the lander and from the surface environment. For an interferometric array such as FARSIDE, the signals from many antennas are combined using their relative timing (phase) to form an image of the sky; the proposed design is described as making a whole-sky image roughly once per minute (Burns et al., 2019). The LuSEE-Night antennas are described as spring-loaded stacer elements that unfold after landing. A turntable is planned to rotate the antenna assembly periodically, so that signals which change after a rotation can be separated from the sky signal, which does not change in the same way (Berkeley Lab, 2023).
article.scientific_importance: The farside is shielded from Earth's radio emissions and from the ionosphere's effects on low-frequency signals, which makes it a distinctive location for radio astronomy at very low frequencies (Burns et al., 2019; Burns et al., 2021; IEEE Spectrum, 2019). The scientific value of a far-side observatory would be greatest if it can measure the 21 cm signal, detect solar-system radio emission continuously and provide calibration data for later arrays. The sources reviewed present these as goals. No published far-side measurement of the Dark Ages signal is cited in this article.

physical_specifications.note: There is no single universal specification for a far-side radio observatory. Concepts range from a few-antenna pathfinder to a multi-kilometre array. The examples below describe specific instruments and concepts and should not be compared as if they were the same design.

examples.name: LuSEE-Night (Lunar Surface Electromagnetics Experiment)
examples.type: Planned flight radio telescope (pathfinder); NASA and US Department of Energy
examples.status: Planned, not flown, as of the sources reviewed. Launch date unresolved (2025 in the 2023 Berkeley Lab article; 2027 in Wikipedia; no earlier than 2027 on the Firefly page).
examples.description: A NASA and US Department of Energy radio experiment planned to fly on Firefly Aerospace's Blue Ghost Mission 2 lander under NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) programme. It is designed to measure low-frequency radio emission from the farside and to act as a pathfinder for the 21 cm Dark Ages measurement.
examples.antennas: Two antenna elements, each about 6 m from tip to tip. Bale et al. (2023) describe two orthogonal electric dipoles; the Berkeley Lab article describes two pairs of antennas. The element count has not been reconciled between these descriptions.
examples.stowage: The antennas must fit in a cube about 1 m on each side for transport and unfold after landing (spring-loaded stacer elements).
examples.receiver: A four-channel baseband receiver system with 50 MHz Nyquist sampling (Bale et al., 2023).
examples.frequency_range_reported: 0.5 to 50 MHz (Berkeley Lab, 2023); below 50 MHz (Firefly page).
examples.mass_notes: Total instrument mass not stated. The only mass figure is for the battery, about 50 kg, which sustains the experiment through the lunar night (Berkeley Lab, 2023).
examples.power_notes: Total instrument power not stated in the sources reviewed.
examples.performance: No sensitivity, calibration or noise figures are published in the sources reviewed.
examples.operating_conditions: Lunar night temperatures of about -280 F (about -173 C) and lunar day temperatures of about 250 F (about 121 C), with the batteries recharging during the day (Berkeley Lab, 2023). Operation on the farside, which never faces Earth, requires relay of data through a satellite.
examples.operating_duration: 18 months of data collection (Berkeley Lab, 2023). The Firefly page gives up to two years. These statements are not reconciled.
examples.relay: ESA Lunar Pathfinder satellite, deployed into lunar orbit by Firefly's Elytra spacecraft (Firefly page).

examples.name: FARSIDE
examples.type: Proposed interferometric low-frequency array (decadal survey concept)
examples.status: Proposed concept; design study. Not built or flown.
examples.description: A proposed far-side low-frequency interferometric array described in a 2019 Astro2020 decadal survey whitepaper. All figures below are design goals from a notional architecture and are not measured values.
examples.element_type: dual-polarisation antennas (Burns et al., 2019); described in Burns et al. (2021) as 128 dipole-antenna pairs
examples.frequency_range_design_goal: 100 kHz to 40 MHz, channelised into 1,400 channels
examples.architecture: A rover deploys the antennas; a base station provides central processing, power and data transmission to the Lunar Gateway, and the antennas are tethered to it.
examples.precursor: A six-element prototype named PRIME is described as a risk-reduction array (Burns et al., 2021).
examples.mass_notes: Not stated in the abstracts reviewed. A search summary reported an estimated payload mass of 1750 kg, but this was not confirmed in full text and is not used.
examples.power_notes: Not stated in the abstracts reviewed.
examples.performance: Angular resolution and sensitivity are not stated in the abstract reviewed; the full paper was not readable in this run.

examples.name: Chang'e-4 Low Frequency Spectrometer
examples.type: Flown radio spectrometer on a lunar farside lander
examples.status: Flown on the Chang'e-4 lander on the farside. Specifications were not found in the sources reviewed; post-2019 operating status not confirmed.
examples.description: The IEEE Spectrum article of December 2019 reports that the Chang'e-4 lander carried a Low Frequency Spectrometer on the lunar farside, similar to NCLE, and notes that the Moon shields it from Earth's electromagnetic interference.
examples.antennas: Not specified in the sources reviewed.
examples.frequency_range: Not specified in the sources reviewed.
examples.performance: Not specified in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: Netherlands-China Low-frequency Explorer (NCLE)
examples.type: Flown radio instrument on the Queqiao relay satellite (Earth-Moon L2, not the lunar surface)
examples.status: Launched with Queqiao. As of the December 2019 IEEE Spectrum article, deployment was partial and observations were about to start. Later status not confirmed.
examples.description: A Dutch-Chinese low-frequency radio instrument carried on the Chinese Queqiao relay satellite, which orbits the second Earth-Moon Lagrange point, about 60,000 to 80,000 km beyond the Moon. It was developed in the Netherlands by Radboud University, ASTRON and ISISpace.
examples.antennas: Three antennas, each described as about 5 m long. Antenna type not specified in the article.
examples.frequency_range_target: 1 to 30 MHz (IEEE Spectrum, 2019). A search summary gave 80 kHz to 80 MHz from another source; not reconciled.
examples.deployment_status_2019: One antenna had nearly reached full length; two were stuck at about 2.5 m (IEEE Spectrum, 2019).
examples.performance: No results reported in the sources reviewed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The LuSEE-Night antennas are about 6 m tip to tip and stow in a cube about 1 m on a side. FARSIDE is a 10 km footprint array of 128 antennas. NCLE antennas are about 5 m long, and the Chang'e-4 spectrometer's dimensions are not given. These examples differ in scale and architecture and should not be compared directly. Dimensions for a new far-side observatory would depend on its frequency range, sensitivity target and deployment method.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Total LuSEE-Night mass is not stated. Its battery is about 50 kg (Berkeley Lab, 2023). FARSIDE mass is not stated in the abstracts reviewed, and no other mass is cited for the other examples. Mass drives lander capacity, so it must be verified for any specific design before transportation planning.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: LuSEE-Night's power comes from a battery that sustains operation through the lunar night and recharges during the lunar day (Berkeley Lab, 2023). Total instrument power is not stated. FARSIDE's power comes from its base station, but no value is given in the abstract reviewed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A farside radio observatory must survive lunar night temperatures of about -280 F (about -173 C) and lunar day temperatures of about 250 F (about 121 C), as reported for LuSEE-Night (Berkeley Lab, 2023). It must operate on the farside, which never faces Earth, so its data must be relayed through a satellite. Power must be stored to carry the instrument through the lunar night. Electrical noise from the lander, the lunar surface and nearby equipment can contaminate low-frequency measurements, so antenna placement, isolation and calibration are central engineering requirements. The Firefly page states that the Blue Ghost lander powers down before lunar night so that it does not interfere with LuSEE-Night (Firefly page). For FARSIDE, environmental and operational requirements are not defined in the sources reviewed.
article.limitations: Any electrical noise from the lander or lunar surface can contaminate low-frequency measurements. The Milky Way and other sources are much brighter than the Dark Ages signal, so that measurement depends on calibration and modelling. A single antenna set on one lander cannot form images of the sky; imaging requires an array such as FARSIDE. LuSEE-Night launch dates vary between sources. NCLE's partial deployment illustrates how mechanical deployment can limit science.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Far-side radio observatories can be delivered to the farside as a single lander payload (LuSEE-Night) or as a rover-deployed array with a base station (FARSIDE, proposed). Flown examples have so far used landers or a relay satellite.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument on the Blue Ghost Mission 2 lander, mounted on the lander's top deck (Firefly page).
Launch and transfer to lunar orbit and the farside landing site, as planned under NASA's CLPS programme.
Land on the farside; the LuSEE-Night antennas unfold from their transport stowage in a cube about 1 m on a side (Berkeley Lab, 2023).
Establish the relay link through ESA's Lunar Pathfinder satellite, which Firefly's Elytra spacecraft deploys into lunar orbit (Firefly page).
Operate the instrument through lunar day and night, using battery power through the night (Berkeley Lab, 2023).
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: LuSEE-Night's antennas are spring-loaded stacer elements that unfold after landing. FARSIDE would use a rover to deploy its 128 antennas across about 10 km and a base station tethered to the Lunar Gateway (Burns et al., 2019). Deployment is therefore a major engineering risk for both concepts. NCLE's antenna deployment stalled at about 2.5 m for two of its three antennas as of December 2019 (IEEE Spectrum, 2019).
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Chang'e-4 lander carried a low-frequency spectrometer to the farside, and NCLE was carried on the Queqiao relay satellite (IEEE Spectrum, 2019). Neither is a precedent for a lander-mounted antenna deployment of LuSEE-Night's type, and their deployment outcomes differ.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Firefly's page supports the claim that LuSEE-Night is hosted on Blue Ghost Mission 2 and mounted on its top deck. Compatibility at the level of mass, mounting loads, power and data interfaces was not verified against mission interface documents. The FARSIDE delivery vehicle is not identified in the abstracts reviewed, and no lander compatibility is asserted for it.

article.historical_significance: The FARSIDE concept was proposed in a 2019 decadal survey whitepaper (Burns et al., 2019). In 2019 the Chang'e-4 lander carried a low-frequency spectrometer to the farside, and NCLE on the Queqiao relay satellite was about to begin observations, with partial antenna deployment problems at the time (IEEE Spectrum, 2019). A 2021 review placed LuSEE and ROLSES within the NASA landed-payload programme as routes to low-frequency lunar radio astronomy (Burns et al., 2021). LuSEE-Night was described in 2023 as a pathfinder for the Dark Ages measurement, with NASA and DOE collaboration (Bale et al., 2023; Berkeley Lab, 2023).
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: LuSEE-Night is planned, not flown, as of the sources reviewed, and its launch date is unresolved. Its operating duration is given as 18 months by Berkeley Lab (2023) and as up to two years by Firefly; these are not reconciled. Its frequency band is given as 0.5 to 50 MHz (Berkeley Lab) and as below 50 MHz (Firefly). Bale et al. (2023) state a 50 MHz Nyquist sampling rate, which would imply a band of roughly 0 to 25 MHz, but they do not state the band directly, so that inference is not used. The LuSEE-Night antenna description differs between sources (orthogonal dipoles versus two pairs). FARSIDE mass and power are not stated in the abstracts reviewed. The 1750 kg figure from a search summary was not verified and is not used. No sensitivity, calibration or noise figures are cited for any instrument. NCLE's target frequency range (1 to 30 MHz) differs from a search-summary range (80 kHz to 80 MHz); this is not reconciled. The Chang'e-4 spectrometer has no specifications in the sources reviewed, and its post-2019 status is not confirmed. No direct image asset URL was verified, so all images are linked to their source pages. The FARSIDE and LuSEE PDFs could not be read in full in this run, so claims rely on abstracts and secondary articles.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No image_url is set because no direct asset URL was verified in this run; each image is linked to its source page. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: LuSEE-Night launch date conflicts across sources: 2025 (Berkeley Lab, 2023), 2027 (Wikipedia), no earlier than 2027 (Firefly page). Current status not confirmed.
LuSEE-Night operating duration conflicts: 18 months (Berkeley Lab, 2023) versus up to two years (Firefly page).
LuSEE-Night antenna description differs between Bale et al. (2023) (two orthogonal electric dipoles, about 6 m tip to tip) and the Berkeley Lab article (two pairs of antennas, six metres tip to tip).
LuSEE-Night frequency band: 0.5 to 50 MHz (Berkeley Lab, 2023); below 50 MHz (Firefly page). Bale et al. state 50 MHz Nyquist sampling, which is not the same as a stated band.
NCLE target range 1 to 30 MHz (IEEE Spectrum, 2019) versus 80 kHz to 80 MHz (search summary from another source). Not reconciled.
A 1750 kg FARSIDE payload mass appeared in a search summary attributed to arXiv:2102.02331. It was not confirmed in the abstract read and is excluded from the JSON numeric fields.
The 2021 arXiv abstract (arXiv:2102.02331) describes FARSIDE as 128 dipole-antenna pairs over 10 km; the 2019 abstract (arXiv:1907.05407) describes 128 dual-polarisation antennas over 10 km.

The full FARSIDE (arXiv:1907.05407) and LuSEE (arXiv:2301.10345) PDFs could not be read in full in this run (no PDF renderer available for the attempted read). Mass, power, angular resolution and sensitivity values are therefore not verified.

Berkeley Lab article URL: the text was read through the Brookhaven National Laboratory reproduction (https://www.bnl.gov/newsroom/news.php?a=221439). That URL includes a query string and was not used; the Berkeley Lab URL was identified from search results and not separately fetched.
The Chang'e-4 Low Frequency Spectrometer has no specifications in the sources reviewed, and its post-2019 operating status is not confirmed.
NCLE is on the Queqiao relay satellite at Earth-Moon L2, not on the lunar surface, so it is classed here as a flown far-side-observing instrument rather than a surface observatory.
No direct image asset URLs were verified. Candidate paths from the Berkeley Lab page (relative to https://www.bnl.gov/today/body_pics/2023/09/) are recorded in image notes only.
Firefly page undated; its footer indicates 2026 and it is treated as a probable mid-2026 snapshot.
Lunar location recommendations are deferred by the user and are not included.
